stages.title: Nature of economics
stages.sub: Why economics studies people rather than particles, and why its models must simplify reality.

steps.q: A physicist studies atoms, which behave the same way every time. An economist studies shoppers, workers and firms deciding what to do. Do people always react the same way to the same event?
steps.wrong: Yes, people always react the same way
steps.hint: Think of two different shoppers facing the same price rise. Will they definitely do the same thing?

steps.right: No, the real economy cannot be repeated like that
steps.wrong: Yes, governments can rerun the economy to test policies

steps.q: Since economists cannot run lab experiments on the real economy, how might they still test an idea about how people behave, such as what happens to spending when income rises?
steps.right: Build a simplified picture of the situation and see what it predicts
steps.wrong: Wait and observe the real economy with no simplification at all
steps.hint: If you cannot experiment on the real thing, what smaller stand-in could you build instead?

steps.q: A model of how much pizza people buy would have to account for price, income, advertising, weather, rivals' prices and dozens of other things at once. Could the model stay useful if it tried to include every single one of these in full detail?
steps.right: No, it would become too complicated to use
steps.wrong: Yes, more detail always makes a model more useful
steps.hint: Think about trying to solve a problem with fifty variables at once versus a handful.

steps.q: You want to see how a rise in the price of pizza alone affects the quantity bought. Income, tastes and rivals' prices are all changing too. If you assume all of those stay fixed while only price changes, what have you achieved?
steps.right: Isolated the effect of price alone
steps.wrong: Made the model less accurate by ignoring real changes
